For there can be no doubt that the extraordinary disharmony of the human being—both anatomical and physiological—the extraordinary unevenness in the development and wearing-out of organs and tissues, gives the instinct for life that cramped, pathological, hysterical form we call the fear of death: a fear that clouds reason and feeds stupid and degrading fantasies about an afterlife.

Human beings will set themselves the task of becoming masters of their own feelings, of raising their instincts to the highest level of consciousness and making them transparently clear, of extending the guiding threads of the will beneath the threshold of consciousness, and in this way of raising themselves to a higher level of awareness.
In other words, humanity will create a higher social-biological type—or, if one prefers, a superhuman.
The average human being will rise to the level of an Aristotle, a Goethe, a Marx.
Above that mountain ridge, new peaks will rise.”
“Hail to you, resplendent earth” — From Richard Wagner, Siegfried, Act III, Scene 3. A piano reduction survives in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 No. 26258.
In Dostoevsky, Kirillov says … — Schmitt quotes Dostoevsky from Walter Schubart, Dostojewski und Nietzsche. Symbolik ihres Lebens, Lucerne 1939, p. 47.
In Dostoevsky, according to E. K. Rahsin’s translation, the sentence reads:
“Man will be God and will change physically.”
Fyodor M. Dostoevsky, Die Dämonen, trans. E. K. Rahsin, Frankfurt am Main, c. 1992, p. 155.
Renan said — Ernest Renan (1823–1892), French scholar of religion and historian.
Renan made this often-repeated remark to the nationalist politician Paul Déroulède in 1883.
To Hans Beyer — Hans Joachim Beyer (1908–1971), historian and active National Socialist. He was an SS-Hauptsturmführer and a close associate of Reinhard Heydrich.
In 1940 he became a professor at Friedrich Wilhelm University in Berlin, in 1941 at Posen, and in 1943 at Prague.
After the war he became press spokesman for the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Schleswig-Holstein, and from 1951 he was a professor at the teacher-training college in Flensburg.

For more on him, see Stephan Linck, Neue Anfänge? Der Umgang der Evangelischen Kirche mit der NS-Vergangenheit und ihr Verhältnis zum Judentum. Die Landeskirchen in Nordelbien, Vol. 1, 1945–1965, Kiel 2013.
Beyer’s letter of 12 June 1948, to which Schmitt was replying, survives in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 No. 1318.
“Haecker’s thought … a more genuinely Catholic sharpening” — The correct passage reads:
“On closer examination, however, Haecker’s thought now belongs essentially to the Catholic literary movement as well.

It did not arise from that movement, because Haecker entered it as an outsider. Nor did it take part in the movement’s earlier opposition between a ‘classicist’ neutralization and a ‘Gothic’ realization.
But it is now struggling toward a more genuinely Catholic sharpening.

The movement itself is in many places turning, out of a barrenness in its creaturely and historical understanding, from the Word to language, from particularity to universality, and from a neutralized form of life to political confession. Much the same can also be said more generally about the intellectual and artistic decisions of the older generation.
Haecker’s thought now takes part in this struggle toward a more genuinely Catholic sharpening.”
Konrad Weiß, “Die Kreatur des Wortes,” in Der Ring (Berlin) 4, 1931, No. 48, p. 902.
Reprinted in Literaturwissenschaftliches Jahrbuch der Görres-Gesellschaft, New Series 12, 1971, pp. 311–315.
On Güllich — Hans Güllich, a first lieutenant on the Eastern Front during the Second World War.
Schmitt is referring to Güllich’s text titled “Lagebeurteilung,” which Güllich sent to Jünger and Jünger passed on to Schmitt.
Wilhelm Schmitz — (1912–?), jurist and industrialist who supported Schmitt after 1945.
See W. Schmitz, “Zur Geschichte der Academia Moralis,” in Schmittiana IV, 1994, pp. 119–156.
G. Radbruch’s favorable review of this book — Karl Schultes’s Der Niedergang des staatsrechtlichen Denkens im Faschismus, Weimar 1947; see the note above to p. 103.
Gustav Radbruch praised it in the Süddeutsche Juristenzeitung, Vol. 3, No. 5, 1948, pp. 223 f., as
“a work much needed for the cleansing of political thought. Heine’s phrase ‘No talent, but character’ could be applied here in reverse.”
“Idea and Reality of the Free German League” — Ernst Rudolf Huber, Idee und Realität eines Freideutschen Bundes, typescript in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 No. 20250.
See Schmitt’s letter to Huber of 18 June 1948, BW Huber, pp. 327–332.
Robert Brasillach — (1909–1945), French writer, executed for collaboration on 6 February 1945.
Gebhard — Klaus Gebhard (1896–1976), Wuppertal manufacturer and art collector, and a friend of Ernst Jünger and Gerhard Nebel.
Ernst Jünger often says … — Jünger does not write this under 9 December, but under 14 December 1943 in Strahlungen:
“Of all the minds I have known, Carl Schmitt is the one who can define things best.”
Privy Councillor am Zehnhoff — Hugo am Zehnhoff (1855–1930), jurist and politician, Prussian minister of justice from 1919 to 1927.
During his time as a lawyer at the Higher Regional Court in Düsseldorf, Carl Schmitt served his legal traineeship under him.
Before moving to Berlin in 1928, Schmitt also stayed at am Zehnhoff’s ministerial residence when visiting Berlin.
Poor in deeds and rich in thought — From Friedrich Hölderlin’s poem “An die Deutschen” (“To the Germans”), second version.
In Hölderlin, Gedichte, based on the historical-critical edition of F. Zinkernagel, Leipzig, no date, p. 125:
Never mock the child when, foolish still, astride its wooden horse, it thinks itself glorious and great. O good people! We too are poor in deeds and rich in thought!
Genoveva’s realm of sorrows — Robert Schumann’s opera Genoveva.
Kaete Eisler — (1898–?), first wife of Schmitt’s friend Georg Eisler.
See Reinhard Mehring, Die Hamburger Verlegerfamilie Eisler und Carl Schmitt, Plettenberger Miniaturen 2, Plettenberg 2009.
Sunt nobis nulla profecto Numina — “For us, there are certainly no gods.” Pharsalia VII, 445 f.
sed victa Catoni — See the note above to p. 79.
Sanctus Cato = nec sancto caruisset vita Catone — “nor would holy Cato have lost his life.” Pharsalia VI, 311.

surdae aures Coelicolum = Inpia tot populis, tot surdas gentibus aures Coelicolum dirae convertunt carmina gentis — “The godless spells of this accursed people reach the ears of the gods, though those ears are deaf to so many nations.” Pharsalia VI, 443 f.
Quis labor sit Superis cantus herbasque sequendi — “Why do the gods above take such trouble to obey incantations and herbs?” Pharsalia VI, 492.

Mortalia nulli Sunt curata Deo. Cladis tamen huius habemus vindictam, quantam terris dare numina fas est — “No god concerns himself with the fate of mortals. Yet the gods have paid for this catastrophe, as far as gods are able to make payment to mortals.” Pharsalia VII, 454–456.
Mentimur regnare Jovem — “We lie when we say that Jupiter rules.” Pharsalia VII, 447.
Hellingr., Vol. VI, p. 120 — Friedrich Hölderlin, Sämtliche Werke, begun by Norbert von Hellingrath and continued by Friedrich Seebass and Ludwig von Pigenot, Vol. 6, Berlin 1923.
The quotation appears at the beginning of Pharsalia.
But I will cultivate within myself the seed of freedom … — From Theodor Däubler, Das Nordlicht, Geneva edition, Leipzig 1922, Vol. 2, Die Auferstehung des Fleisches, p. 495.
Jamjam hiscit flammeus — “At once the flames blaze up.”
Nicolaus Sombart’s Capriccio — N. Sombart, Capriccio Nr. 1. Des Wachsoldaten Irrungen und Untergang, Frankfurt am Main 1947.
Walter Fuchs — (1888–1966), diplomat and friend of Schmitt from his Munich years.

See P. Tommissen, “Bausteine zu einer wiss. Biographie,” in Complexio oppositorum. Über Carl Schmitt. Vorträge und Diskussionsbeiträge des 28. Sonderseminars 1986 der Hochschule für Verwaltungswissenschaften Speyer, ed. H. Quaritsch, Berlin 1986, p. 79.
I know the dear Germans already, etc. —
“I know the dear Germans well enough: first they keep quiet, then they carp, then they push you aside, then they steal from you and keep silent about you.”
In J. W. Goethe, Gedenkausgabe der Werke, Briefe und Gespräche, ed. Ernst Beutler, 2nd ed., Vol. 22, Zurich 1964, p. 863.
Schmitt quoted the passage repeatedly. See, for example, BW Mohler, p. 182; Tb 1930–34, p. 427.

omnia cedunt in favorem et jus justum bellum gerentium — “Everything gives way to the advantage and the rights of the one who wages a just war.” Francisco de Vitoria, Escuela Española de la Paz. Primera generación 1526–1560, Madrid 1981, p. 336. See also the notes below on pp. 148 and 154.
si licite sunt capta, puto quod non sunt obnoxia restitutioni — “If something has been lawfully seized, I do not think there is any duty to return it.” F. de Vitoria, cited above.

J’ai montré la porte … — Antoine de Rivarol, Maximen, Frankfurt am Main 1956, p. 117. Ernst Jünger translates it as: “I shall therefore not point out the secret entrance to that remote sanctuary where the most delicate and difficult questions of law and morality are decided—all those problems too subtle for the scales of Themis. For if that gate were shown, greed and all the sophistries of passion would soon force their way inside and violate conscience in its last refuge.” E. Jünger, Sämtliche Werke, vol. 14, p. 302. See also Schmitt’s letter to Ernst Jünger of 20 August 1948, in BW EJ, p. 231.
The letter to Forsthoff mentioned here is not included in BW Forsthoff.
Valléry-Radot — Robert Valléry-Radot (1885–1970), French writer and friend of Georges Bernanos and François Mauriac.
Höffner’s book — Joseph Höffner, Christentum und Menschenwürde. Das Anliegen der spanischen Kolonialethik im goldenen Zeitalter, Trier 1947.
Rossini being booed — Rossini’s most famous opera, The Barber of Seville, was booed at its premiere in Rome in 1816.
Golombek — Walter Golombek (1914–?), Schmitt’s assistant at Friedrich Wilhelm University in Berlin. Two letters from him and one from his father survive in the papers; RW 265, nos. 5065–5067.

collaboration with Frank — Hans Frank (1900–1946), lawyer, Reich Minister under the Nazis, and Governor-General of occupied Poland, supported Schmitt during the early years of the Third Reich. Frank was sentenced to death at the main Nuremberg war-crimes trial and executed in 1946.
